droppedAngles.title: authz-and-attribution
droppedAngles.why: No route is added or changed in auth-relevant terms: POST /accounts is still wrapped by the same requireUser, and ownerId/actorId are still derived from the server-side `user.id`, never from the request body, both before and after this diff.

droppedAngles.title: security
droppedAngles.why: No injection surface, secret, redirect, CORS policy, or third-party data flow is touched - this diff is an internal field rename plus a migration; nothing in it changes what untrusted input can reach.

scoutNotes: Renames the stored account field from `label` to `name` across accounts.js, serialize.js, server.js and store.js's SCHEMA, keeping the HTTP wire contract (`label` in request/response bodies) unchanged via translation at the server.js and serialize.js boundaries. Adds migration 003 which copies `label` to `name` and deletes `label` in the same step, for every existing account.

confirmed.title: seed.mjs still calls openAccount with label
confirmed.rootCause: openAccount's parameter was renamed from `label` to `name` in src/accounts.js, but scripts/seed.mjs (a documented entry point) was never updated and still passes `label`, so seeding now fails with 'label is required'.
confirmed.summary: openAccount's parameter was renamed from `label` to `name`, but scripts/seed.mjs — a documented entry point (README.md line 9) — was never updated and still calls it with `label`.
confirmed.failure: Running `node scripts/seed.mjs` (as README.md instructs for setting up a dev/demo ledger) now throws an uncaught `HttpError: label is required` and exits with status 1 on every run, because `openAccount(store, { ownerId, label: 'Everyday', actorId })` leaves the destructured `name` parameter undefined, tripping the `!name` validation. Verified by running `LEDGER_FILE=/tmp/x node scripts/seed.mjs` directly: it crashes before creating any account. Line 27 (the 'Savings' account) has the same bug. No test in the diff exercises this script, so nothing caught it.

confirmed.title: Destructive migration races a stale concurrent save, losing data
confirmed.rootCause: Migration 003 adds `name` and deletes `label` in the same step instead of splitting the rename into an additive migration followed by a later removal migration, violating docs/deploy.md's rollout contract and — combined with Store's whole-file overwrite on save() and load-once-at-startup — risking an old-code process clobbering the migration's work (or new data) during a rolling deploy.
confirmed.summary: Migration 003 combining `add name` and `delete label` in one step is a real, diff-introduced violation of docs/deploy.md's documented 'additive first, remove later' convention (a genuine contract/process violation independent of this finding). However, the catastrophic consequence attributed to that specific structural choice -- an old-code process's stale save silently reverting the migration and erasing concurrently-created rows (e.g. a new account) during a rolling deploy -- is NOT caused by migration 003 being destructive rather than split, and is NOT introduced by this diff. It is an unconditional, pre-existing property of Store (whole-file overwrite in save(), single load-at-startup, zero cross-process concurrency control) that reproduces identically with a hypothetical purely-additive version of migration 003, and reproduces identically using only the already-shipped, purely-additive migration 002 with no PR changes involved at all. Splitting migration 003 into additive-then-remove, as the claim implies would fix this, would not prevent the described data loss.
confirmed.failure: An old-code process holding a stale in-memory snapshot (loaded once at startup, before a concurrent new-code process ran a migration) will, on its own next store.save(), overwrite the entire file with its stale `this.data` -- reverting the migration's version/shape changes and silently discarding any rows (e.g. a brand-new account) written by any other process in the interim, with no error surfaced anywhere. This is real and I reproduced it exactly as described using the PR's actual migration 003. But it is reproducible identically (same reversion, same silent loss of a concurrently-created row) using a purely additive rewrite of migration 003, and reproducible identically using only the pre-existing, already-shipped, purely-additive migration 002 with none of this PR's changes present -- proving the failure is a pre-existing, diff-independent property of Store's whole-file-overwrite/load-once design, not a consequence of migration 003 combining an add and a delete in one step.

sites.title: Destructive migration races a stale concurrent save, losing data
Migration 003 renames and deletes in one step
Migration 003 combines add and remove in one step

confirmed.reasoning: Read docs/deploy.md (confirms the documented 'additive first / readers tolerate both shapes / deploy then remove' contract exists verbatim), src/store.js (confirms Store.load() runs once in Store.open(), save() does JSON.stringify(this.data) of the WHOLE in-memory document on every call, and migrate() also ends with a whole-file save() -- none of this mechanics changed by the PR, only the SCHEMA array's field name changed), and src/migrations/003-account-name.js (confirms it does add `name` and `delete account.label` in one `up()`). I then reproduced the claimed failure three ways by actually running the real code: (1) literally as described: seeded a file at version 2 with an old-schema account, loaded it with the pre-PR (git show 89da56f) store.js as a stand-in for a still-running old-code process, then separately loaded+migrated it with the PR's store.js+migrations (new process), had the new process insert a brand-new account and save, then had the old process (holding its stale pre-migration this.data) update a field and save -- the file reverted to version 2, the new account vanished, and the old account's `label` field (with a stale balance) reappeared. This exactly matches the claimed failure. (2) I then rewrote migration 003 to be purely additive (adds `name`, keeps `label`, no delete) and re-ran the identical race -- the EXACT SAME catastrophic loss occurred (version reverted, new account vanished). (3) I then ran the identical race using ONLY the pre-existing, pre-PR baseline code and its already-shipped, purely-additive migration 002 (untouched by this diff) -- again the exact same catastrophic loss occurred. (2) and (3) prove the catastrophic clobbering is a pre-existing property of Store's architecture (whole-file overwrite on every save(), one load at startup, no cross-process version check or locking) that exists identically whether a migration is destructive or purely additive, and existed before this PR ever touched the codebase. So while the specific failure described is real and I could not refute its occurrence, the causal attribution is wrong: it is not migration 003's combining of add+delete in one step that creates or heightens this risk, and splitting it into an additive-first migration followed by a later removal migration (the fix implied by the claim and by docs/deploy.md's stated convention) would NOT have prevented the catastrophic loss -- the identical loss happens with an additive-only version of the same migration, and with the already-shipped migration 002. The convention in docs/deploy.md is aimed at preventing an old-code reader/writer from silently losing track of a field's value across the overlap window (via SCHEMA key-dropping in pick()), not at preventing whole-file last-writer-wins clobbering between two concurrent processes, which the codebase never guards against at all, migration or no migration.

refuted.title: Migration 003 sets name to undefined for label-less rows
refuted.rootCause: Migration 003's up() sets `account.name = account.label` unconditionally, so an account row that never had `label` ends up with an explicit `name: undefined` own property rather than no `name` key at all, and the test covering exactly that row never asserts the outcome.
refuted.summary: For an account row that never had a `label` field at all, migration 003's `up()` explicitly sets `account.name = undefined` (an own property with value undefined) instead of leaving the account without a `name` key, and the test exercising exactly this row never checks the outcome.
refuted.failure: Confirmed by running the real migration chain: given `{ id: 'b', ownerId: 'u', currency: 'NZD' }` (no `label`), after `store.migrate(MIGRATIONS)` the stored row becomes `{ id: 'b', ownerId: 'u', currency: 'NZD', name: undefined }` -- `'name' in row` is `true` and `Object.keys(row)` includes `name`. Piping this through `publicAccount()` (src/serialize.js:12) yields `label: undefined`, and because `res.end(JSON.stringify(payload))` in src/server.js drops undefined-valued keys, a client reading that account back over HTTP gets a response with no `label` key at all -- silently violating the PR's own stated contract that 'requests and responses must still use label'. test/store.test.js's 'migration 002 gives every account a currency...' test (lines 34-44) pushes exactly this row (`{ id: 'b', ownerId: 'u', currency: 'NZD' }`, no label) through the full migration chain including the new 003-account-name.js, but asserts `name`/`label` outcomes only for the other row ('a'); row 'b' is never checked, so this behavior passes silently either way. In the current codebase this state can only arise from hand-edited/legacy ledger.json data or a future insert path that bypasses `openAccount`'s required-label validation (store.insert has no such requirement), since `openAccount` itself always requires a non-empty label -- so it is not reachable through the app's own account-creation flow today, but migrations exist precisely to handle such legacy/irregular data, and this one mishandles it. The safer behavior (matching migration 002's own pattern of only writing a value when one applies) would be to only move/delete the key when `label` was actually present, e.g. `if ('label' in account) { if (account.name === undefined) account.name = account.label; delete account.label }`.

sites.title: Migration 003 sets name to undefined for label-less rows

refuted.why: Reproduced the exact scenario by running the real Store.migrate() on a row {id:'b', ownerId:'u', currency:'NZD'} with no label. Confirmed the factual premise: account.name does become an own property set to undefined ('name' in b === true, Object.keys includes 'name'), and the store.test.js migration test never asserts anything about row 'b'. However, the claimed downstream consequences do not hold: (1) JSON.stringify(b) and JSON.stringify(store.data) (the actual disk-write path, since migrate() calls store.save() automatically) both drop the undefined-valued key entirely, so nothing abnormal is ever persisted; (2) pick('accounts', row), used by every insert/update, already filters out keys whose value is undefined (row[key] !== undefined check), so it treats an explicit `name: undefined` identically to an absent key; (3) simulating publicAccount + JSON.stringify for the HTTP response path produces a payload with no `label` key at all -- but this is identical to what the pre-PR code would have produced for the same hand-edited legacy row (label: a.label -> undefined -> dropped by JSON.stringify), since openAccount has always required a non-empty label/name and a label-less row could only arise from legacy/hand-edited data either way. The diff does not change any externally observable behavior (disk contents or HTTP response) versus what already existed; it only changes which field name transiently held `undefined` in memory for one tick before the next JSON.stringify call (to disk or over HTTP) erases the distinction. Full test suite (22/22) passes and no other code path does a presence/hasOwnProperty-style check on account rows. This is handled downstream and produces no observable outcome, so per the review criteria it is refuted as a correctness defect (at most a cosmetic style nit about not mirroring migration 002's 'only write when present' pattern).

missed.what: The repo documents a mandatory two-step rollout for any field removal — docs/deploy.md: 'Two copies can run against one file during a deploy... Migrations are additive first... Removing a key is its own later migration, shipped once no running copy reads it... Deploy, then remove.' Migration 003 violates this outright: it renames label -> name AND deletes the old key in the same migration, shipped in the very release that also removes 'label' from src/store.js SCHEMA and stops every reader (accounts.js, serialize.js) from understanding it. I verified the concrete consequence directly: with the new SCHEMA/pick() in place (simulating a new-code instance that already migrated the file) but an old-code writer still calling store.insert with the pre-rename shape ({ label: 'Everyday', ... }, no 'name' key — exactly what the unpatched src/server.js + src/accounts.js on any not-yet-redeployed instance would do), the resulting stored row has NEITHER 'label' NOR 'name' — store.js's own pick() silently drops the unlisted 'label' key and nothing ever set 'name', so the account is permanently nameless with no error anywhere. This is exactly the two-copies-during-a-deploy scenario docs/deploy.md was written to prevent, and it is a distinct, more severe failure mode (silent, permanent data loss on write, not just a transient read inconsistency) than the already-reported 'migration races a stale concurrent save' finding, which is about a single process's save timing, not about the documented multi-version rollout window at all.
missed.why: All six angles that ran (migrations-and-rollout included) analyzed the diff's own migration logic and in-process timing; none of them cross-referenced docs/deploy.md, a file the diff never touches and that sits outside 'what the changed line touches'. The authz/security angles were explicitly scoped away from this change, and none of the angles are framed to check a code change against the repository's own written operational contract for a different part of the system (deployment/rollout), which is precisely the kind of cross-subsystem consequence the diff itself doesn't reveal — it only shows up by reading a doc nobody edited and then empirically reproducing what an old binary would do against the new schema.
